display.title: Im Yirtzeh Hashem: The Chassid Who Was Sent to Siberia
display.summary_short: A lesson from the spies in Parshas Shelach about trusting Hashem, and a story of the Alter Rebbe's Chassid who learned the hard way to always say "Im Yirtzeh Hashem."
display.summary_long: After the song "I Believe in Hashem," the storyteller asks why the Torah tells us about the spies in Parshas Shelach. Their mistake was thinking the giants of Canaan were stronger than Hashem, and the Torah tells it so that we learn to trust Hashem. Mistakes can become treasures when we learn from them, like a boy who gets his shoe wet at the pond and is more careful next time. That is why Yidden say "Im Yirtzeh Hashem" about every plan. Then comes the story: in the days of the Alter Rebbe, a Chassid named Reb Moshe, with the Rebbe's approval, borrows a thousand rubles from friends to lend a poritz who wants to become an officer in Petersburg. When Reb Moshe comes to collect, the new officer has him arrested and sent to Siberia. A window shut in his face turns out to save him, when the Tsarina frees everyone still waiting in line. She makes the officer pay and dismisses him. The Alter Rebbe explains why Reb Moshe suffered: he had promised his friends repayment without saying "Im Yirtzeh Hashem."
display.lesson: Nothing happens without Hashem wanting it, so always say "Im Yirtzeh Hashem" and trust Him; even what looks bad can be for our good, and we can learn from mistakes.
